response.title: home battery backup for power outages
response.answer:
For home battery backup during power outages, there are three main options, depending on whether you want to keep a few essential devices running or power your entire house.

1. Choose the type of backup system
Shop

Portable battery power station

Best for essential devices

Typically $500–$4,000+

Plug in a refrigerator, router, lights, or medical equipment. No permanent installation required for ordinary plug-in use.

Shop

Whole-home battery backup

Typically $10,000–$20,000+ installed for a single battery system.

Automatically powers selected circuits or potentially the entire house during an outage. Requires professional installation.

Shop

Expandable battery system

Typically $2,000–$10,000+, depending on capacity and installation.

Start with essential appliances, then add batteries. Some systems support a transfer switch or home electrical panel integration.

2. How much battery capacity do you need?

Battery capacity is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). The larger the capacity, the longer your devices can run.

Here is an interactive estimate for an outage:

Battery capacity

4 kWh

Average electricity consumption

150 W — Fridge, Wi-Fi, a few lights
400 W — Multiple essential appliances
1,000 W — Larger household loads
2,500 W — High household consumption

Estimated backup runtime

8.5 hours
Assumes 85% usable energy after losses, constant average load, and no recharging. Actual results vary.
3. Battery systems worth considering

EcoFlow - DELTA 3 Ultra (3072 Wh Capacity) Portable Power St…

3.07 kWh / 3,600 W output

$1,299.00

Good for essential appliances without permanent installation.

EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Portable Power Station

4.1 kWh / 4,000 W output

$3,399.00

Supports 120/240 V output and expandable storage.

Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus + Smart Home Power Kit

3.84 kWh / 6,000 W output

$4,799.99

Home-panel integration option; professional installation costs extra.

For outages lasting several days, consider a solar-rechargeable system. A battery alone eventually runs out, regardless of its size.

## 2. How much battery capacity do you need?

Battery capacity is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). The larger the capacity, the longer your devices can run.

Here is an interactive estimate for an outage:

{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState(4)}
{@body const [load,setLoad] = DIL.useState("400")}
{@body const runtime = capacity*0.85/(Number(load)/1000)}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <box gap={1}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      **Battery capacity**
      <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{capacity} kWh</text>
    </row>
    <slider min={1} max={30} step={1} value={capacity} onChange={setCapacity}/>
  </box>
  <box gap={1}>
    **Average electricity consumption**
    <radio-group direction="col" value={load} onChange={setLoad}>
      <radio value="150">150 W — Fridge, Wi-Fi, a few lights</radio>
      <radio value="400">400 W — Multiple essential appliances</radio>
      <radio value="1000">1,000 W — Larger household loads</radio>
      <radio value="2500">2,500 W — High household consumption</radio>
    </radio-group>
  </box>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="lg" gap={1}>
    <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">Estimated backup runtime</text>
    <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{runtime>=24 ? `${(runtime/24).toFixed(1)} days` : `${runtime.toFixed(1)} hours`}</title>
    <caption>Assumes 85% usable energy after losses, constant average load, and no recharging. Actual results vary.</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Battery bank or generator? How to choose the best backup power for your home during an outage
search_results.snippet: Choosing backup power depends on outage length, household needs and budget. Portable battery banks, usually under $100, are convenient for phones, computers and lights but cannot run major appliances. Fuel-powered portable generators can operate refrigerators, fans and some air conditioners for roughly 6–12 hours or longer, but must be used outdoors to prevent carbon-monoxide poisoning; fuel costs, maintenance and limited tank capacity are concerns during prolonged outages.
